newsitem.title: UK: Shell gets caught in Nigerian political cross-fire.
newsitem.headline: Shell gets caught in Nigerian political cross-fire.

text.p: Oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell has got caught up in the political cross-fire again -- but this time not of its own making.
Still reeling from a bruising tussle with the green lobby over how to dispose of North Sea oil rigs in 1995, the company has been unexpectedly swept up in a political storm in Nigeria.
Nigerian villagers near the oil town of Warri are still holding 96 people hostages who work for the company in a dispute over local government.
But this time at least, the row has nothing to do with the oil giant which has been sucked into negotiating the hostages release.
Over a hundred hostages were taken last weekend when six pumping stations were overrun by villagers protesting the relocation of their local government headquarters. Some 31 were released on Tuesday.
"They (Shell) got caught up. There is an inherent risk in working in that type of environment," said Scott Carter, senior oil trader at Tosco Corp.
Shell said it has lost 100,000 barrels per day of production, just under five percent of Nigeria's total output, but that it had not affected its exports.
Last November Steve Ollerearnshaw, in charge of Shell's operations in Warri, west of the Niger river, perhaps foretold last weekend's events.
"The government is in the oil business and the oil industry is in local government," he said last year.
Oil production for Shell in Nigeria is easy. But very little else is.

Some 16 months after the execution of author and minority rights campaigner Ken Saro-Wiwa at the hands of Nigeria's military rulers, the oil-rich swamps of the Niger river delta still present the Anglo-Dutch multinational with the knottiest of dilemmas.
What are its responsibilities in a developing country with few social services and little local infrastructure?
Shell is in Nigeria because the country supplies more crude than any other of its operations, has huge and easily extractable reserves and provides a clear profit of more than $220 million a year.
Ideally the company is keen to divide politics from economics but admits that on the ground it is not that simple, partly because it is seen as the only source of social amenities.

Scores of rural communities across the delta target Shell, accusing the company of environmental damage and stealing their birthright. But the underlying issue for the tribesmen living next to Shell since oil started flowing in 1958, that of simple living standards, has barely been addressed.
The government, which relies on oil exports for 90 percent of foreign change revenues, has failed to redistribute multi-billion dollar annual earnings to its people.

The state oil company NNPC is struggling to finance its 55 percent share in the joint venture consortium run by Shell, running up huge debts, and has been accused of scuppering new developments and denying funds to smooth community relations.
Shell, caught in the middle, admits that until recently it did not do enough to contain growing resentment among the communities which flared into violence in 1993 and 1994.
The company fled Ogoniland in the eastern delta in 1993 amid sabotage and attacks on its staff. In the west, a three-day siege of Shell's Warri compound brought executives to the negotiating table.
Earlier this month Shell published revised business principles, incorporating respect for human rights for the first time.

Shell's spending on community assistance, to schools, hospitals and the like has risen sharply in the past two years. Community spending increased to $30 million in 1996 with another $90 million spent on the environment.
The company says it easily outspends the government in the delta. As a result, oil production lost to sabotage and other community disturbances has been reduced sharply from its peak in 1994.
